endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Determine whether there is an accessible, easy-tounderstand way for affected groups to know that part of their treatment was determined by an AI solution and also note whether providing this information could increase the risk of harm or reduce the potential benefit.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: regarding transparency and disclosure of the use of AI should be based upon a risk- and impact-based approach that considers the unique circumstance of AI and its use case.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Perform AI red-teaming to assess resilience against: Abuse to facilitate attacks on other systems (e.g., malicious code generation, enhanced phishing content), GAI attacks (e.g., prompt injection)

endorsements.title: Lessons from Henrietta Lacks inform a transparency framework to catalyze generative artificial intelligence in medicine
endorsements.quote: This commitment to transparency should be tailored to the specific state of AI implementation.

endorsements.title: Legal implications of AI standard of care integration on patients’ informed consent: lessons from surgery
endorsements.quote: Instead on focusing on information for disclosure’s sake, informed consent discussions should remain focused on empowering patient autonomy by providing information that is relevant to patients ’ decisions in situations when patients have a meaningful choice .

endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: Health equity stakeholders are increasingly calling for governance that includes bias audits and transparency reporting in healthcare AI, with audit logs ideally including stratified analyses by patient demographics to detect and mitigate such disparities11.

endorsements.title: Early Online
endorsements.issuer: South African medical journal = Suid-Afrikaanse tydskrif vir geneeskunde
endorsements.quote: Low‑risk AI (administrative functions without clinical inference): use should be recorded, with minimal disclosure provided through standard privacy notices.

evidence.title: Patients' experiences and attitudes toward the use of real-time artificial intelligence-assisted colonoscopy
evidence.venue: Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland
evidence.outcome: Patient views on how much information about AI should be provided
evidence.effect: Patients wanted information about AI proportional to the consequences; written information should be informative but concise, avoiding details that create confusion.
evidence.quote: If written information about AI is provided, it should be informative but concise, avoiding details that generate more confusion than clarity.

evidence.title: Patient perspectives on informed consent for medical AI: A web-based experiment
evidence.outcome: Effect of procedure risk, AI prevalence, and AI superiority on perceived importance of AI information
evidence.effect: High risk raised importance only for opinion_same (b 0.0488, p=0.008) and reason_reject_accept (b 0.0434, p=0.02); commonness and superior performance had no significant effect.
evidence.quote: Surprisingly, neither the pervasiveness of the use of AI ( common ) nor the superior performance of the AI tool compared to an average radiologist ( superior ) had a significant effect on the perceived importance of AI information.

commentary.bottom_line: Four sources endorse scaling AI disclosure to risk, but the two studies that test patient preferences disagree: 20 Danish patients favored information proportional to consequences, while among 1,000 South Korean survey respondents high procedural risk raised the importance of AI information on only two measured items. No study has tested whether risk-tiered disclosure changes patient understanding, trust, or harm in practice.

perspectives.view: The evidence consists of one qualitative focus group (n=20) and one vignette survey (n=1,000). Both measure stated preferences rather than the outcomes of a deployed disclosure policy, and their findings conflict. Given the indirect outcomes, the inconsistency, and the study designs, certainty that risk-calibrated disclosure improves patient understanding or safety is very low.

In the vignette study, high procedural risk raised the importance of two items. One was whether the AI opinion matched the physician's (b 0.0488, p=0.008). The other was the reasons to reject or accept AI output (b 0.0434, p=0.02). This suggests that risk tiers set by procedure type may not track what patients consider material. No study measured errors or harm.

Danish patients in focus groups asked for AI information proportional to the consequences of its use. They wanted written material that is informative and concise and that avoids details that create confusion. Their views support tailoring disclosure. These views come from 20 people in one country.

The Danish study is coded as including non-English speakers. This coding likely reflects its Danish-language setting rather than patients with limited proficiency in the dominant language. Neither study reports Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy participants. Whether concise, risk-scaled disclosure serves patients who need interpreters or plain-language formats remains untested.

Of the four endorsing sources, the CHAI guide and the augmented intelligence principles address risk- and impact-based disclosure directly, both at the should level. The NIST generative AI profile excerpt concerns red-teaming, and the portal messaging commentary concerns bias audits and transparency reporting. Neither of those two excerpts speaks to calibrating disclosure.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared risk-tiered disclosure with uniform disclosure in a live deployment. None has measured patient comprehension, trust, decisions, or reported harm. Future trials or stepped implementations should define materiality tiers in advance. They should test whether patients can act on what they are told. They should also enroll Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy patients.
commentary.underserved_note: One test, the Danish focus group, is coded as including non-English-speaking participants. This coding probably reflects the national language rather than limited English proficiency within a health system. Neither test reports Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy participants. Health systems therefore have no evidence on whether calibrated disclosure reaches or informs these patients as intended.
